scenario_user_message: My knowledge base updates every day — does the industry generally use RAG now, or are there other new approaches?

finalMessages.content: My knowledge base updates every day — does the industry generally use RAG now, or are there other new approaches?

content.text:
Good question, and the daily-update part is exactly the right thing to focus on for this node.

Quick principle first: when your data changes daily, the deciding factor is how the freshness gets into the model's answers. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights — to reflect new data you'd have to retrain or run a new fine-tune job, which you can't realistically do every day in a way that stays current. RAG keeps the knowledge in an external store you can update independently, so a daily-changing source maps very naturally onto it. You re-index, the model retrieves the fresh version. That's why for high-churn data, RAG is the default lean.

On your "are there newer approaches" — let me check what's current rather than guess.

RAG is a method where the model dynamically pulls in external data at inference time. Fine-tuning is the process of modifying a model’s weights during training using labeled data. In real-world systems, the choice between RAG and fine-tuning depends on variables like scale, query volume, and how often your data changes.

content.text:
The search confirms the picture, and surfaces one newer name worth knowing.

For daily-changing knowledge, RAG is indeed the industry default — that hasn't been displaced. The reason maps directly to your situation: you update the index, not the model.

The one newer thing to flag is CAG (cache-augmented generation). Instead of retrieving at query time, it preloads your knowledge into the model's context (using long-context windows and KV-caching) ahead of time. It's faster at inference, but the tradeoff is the opposite of what you want: it shines for stable, bounded knowledge that fits in context and doesn't change much. For a daily-churning base, you'd be rebuilding the cache constantly — so it doesn't really beat RAG for your case.

So the honest answer: for daily updates, RAG remains the right tool, and the "new approaches" don't change that conclusion — they mostly serve the stable-data end of the spectrum.

One thing I'd push on though: "updates every day" can mean very different things. Is it a few new documents added daily, or are existing facts being overwritten/invalidated? The second case is harder — RAG can happily retrieve a stale chunk if you don't actively delete or version the old one. Freshness isn't automatic just because you chose RAG; it depends on your re-indexing and invalidation discipline. Which of those two is closer to your situation?

key_takeaways: For daily-changing data, the deciding factor is how freshness reaches the model's answers — fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights and can't realistically be retrained daily, while RAG keeps knowledge in an external store you can re-index independently.
RAG remains the industry default for high-churn / fast-moving data, and this was confirmed via web search; the newer approaches do not displace it for this use case.

CAG (cache-augmented generation) preloads knowledge into the model's context for faster inference, but it's suited to stable, bounded knowledge — for a daily-churning base you'd be rebuilding the cache constantly, so it doesn't beat RAG here.

Freshness is not automatic with RAG: if existing facts are being overwritten/invalidated, RAG can still retrieve stale chunks unless you actively delete or version old data through good re-indexing and invalidation discipline.
open_questions: Whether the user's 'updates every day' means adding new documents daily or overwriting/invalidating existing facts — the assistant asked but the user hasn't answered, and this affects how hard the freshness problem is.
